Empirical Research Plan – “Inequality and Growth”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary design: Staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) with an event-study specification.

Rationale  
• We observe a long country-panel with plausible “shocks” to inequality generated by large redistributive or deregulatory episodes (e.g. land reforms, tax reforms, minimum-wage hikes, resource booms that favour capital owners).  
• The timing of those shocks differs across countries and decades, giving the required staggered adoption structure.  
• With country and year fixed effects plus time-varying covariates, the design uses within-country changes relative to countries that have not yet (or never) experienced the shock.  
• The event-study coefficients (leads & lags) allow visual and formal pre-trend testing and dynamic treatment-effect estimation.  

Supplementary check: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) using a shift-share instrument – the interaction of (i) pre-sample primary-commodity export shares and (ii) world commodity-price shocks – for the inequality variable.  This helps address measurement error and any remaining simultaneity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treat_it = 1 starting in the first year t* that country i experiences a “large inequality shock,” defined as |ΔGini_i,t*| ≥ 5 points relative to the average Gini in the previous three years and persisting for ≥2 consecutive years.  Treat_it stays 1 afterwards (“ever-treated”), matching the canonical staggered DiD set-up.

Control (counterfactual) group  
Country-years that have not (yet) crossed the threshold at time t.  Never-shocked countries remain pure controls.

Treatment timing / Event date  
t* = first year the 5-point jump is observed.  We omit countries observed for <5 years before t* to allow pre-trend estimation.

Key covariates  
– GDP per-capita (lagged), investment/GDP, human-capital index, polity score, trade-openness, commodity-price exposure, demographics.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends: In the absence of the shock, treated and control countries would have followed the same growth path (conditional on covariates and fixed effects).  
Plausibility: The event-study will test for pre-trend differences.  Because shocks originate from country-specific political/commodity events rather than systematic slowing growth, the assumption is defensible but must be scrutinised.

A2. Exogeneity of treatment timing: The precise year a country crosses the 5-point threshold is not chosen because policymakers could forecast near-term growth.  
Plausibility: Sudden resource-price swings or externally driven crises satisfy this better than gradual reforms; we will classify only “exogenous” shocks (detailed in appendix) as treatment.

A3. Stable composition / no interference (SUTVA): A country’s shock does not directly change another country’s growth except through global year dummies.  
Plausibility: Reasonable given the inclusion of common-year shocks but we will cluster standard errors by country and continent.

A4. No differential measurement error around the event: GDP and Gini measurement quality does not jump at t*.  
Plausibility: Country statistical capacity changes slowly; we will drop years with known survey breaks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous policy shocks  
   – Mitigation:  classify only plausibly exogenous shocks (commodity-price driven; military coups that abruptly redistribute; IMF-mandated VAT reforms) and exclude slow, pre-announced reforms.  Event-study pre-trends provide an empirical test.

T2. Heterogeneous treatment effects biasing TWFE estimators  
   – Mitigation:  implement the Sun & Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted estimator which is robust to heterogeneous effects; repeat with Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) “did” package.

T3. Time-varying confounders (e.g. simultaneous macro crises)  
   – Mitigation:  add country-specific linear time trends; control for terms-of-trade, crisis dummies, democracy transitions; run 2SLS with the shift-share instrument as an alternative.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # TWFE + SunAb
library(did)           # Callaway–Sant’Anna robustness
library(ivreg)         # 2SLS
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------
df_raw <- read_csv("inequality_growth_panel.csv")

# 2. Variable construction -----------------------------------------
df <- df_raw %>% 
  group_by(country) %>% 
  arrange(year) %>% 
  mutate(gini_lag3 = lag(Gini, 1:3) %>% rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE),
         gini_jump = abs(Gini - gini_lag3) >= 5,
         # first year crossing threshold
         treat_year = ifelse(gini_jump & 
                             !lag(cumsum(gini_jump) > 0, default = 0), year, NA),
         treat_year = min(treat_year, na.rm = TRUE),
         treated = ifelse(year >= treat_year, 1, 0),
         time_to_treat = year - treat_year,
         post  = treated,
         ln_gdppc = log(gdppc_const),
         growth = 100 * (ln_gdppc - lag(ln_gdppc))) %>% 
  ungroup()

# 3. Sun & Abraham TWFE event-study --------------------------------
es <- feols(growth ~ sunab(treat_year, year) + 
                  l.invest_gdp + l.human_capital + l.trade_open +
                  l.pop_growth, 
            cluster = ~country, data = df)

summary(es)

iplot(es)   # dynamic plot of coefficients

# 4. 2SLS robustness (shift-share IV) -------------------------------
# First construct instrument: pre-sample commodity share * global price index
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(share_primary80 = share_primary_1980,
         global_price = world_comm_price_index,
         iv_shiftshare = share_primary80 * global_price)

iv_est <- ivreg(growth ~ Gini + controls | iv_shiftshare + controls, data = df)
coeftest(iv_est, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = ~country)

# 5. Callaway–Sant’Anna robustness ---------------------------------
cs <- att_gt(yname = "growth", tname = "year", idname = "country",
             gname = "treat_year", data = df,
             xformla = ~ l.invest_gdp + l.human_capital)
agg_effects <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_effects)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory offers two competing channels:  
• Credit-constraint channel → high inequality lowers aggregate investment in human capital and thus growth, especially in low- and middle-income countries.  
• Incentive / savings channel → inequality could raise growth in very rich countries by fostering capital accumulation.

Overall prior: a 1-point increase in the Gini coefficient is expected to reduce annual per-capita GDP growth by roughly 0.05–0.10 percentage points in countries below the OECD median income; effect near zero or mildly positive in high-income OECD.  We anticipate the average treatment effect (ATE) across the full sample to be negative (≈ –0.07 pp).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Well-defined intervention (large inequality shock) – 1  
C2: Parallel pre-trends supported by event-study – 0.8  
C3: No anticipation/contamination – 0.7  
C4: Correct estimator for staggered adoption – 1  
C5: Robustness to alternative definitions / IV confirmation – 0.8  

(Overall ≈ 4.3 / 5)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan combines a modern staggered DiD/event-study with a complementary IV, explicitly states assumptions, and embeds diagnostics and robustness checks in reproducible R code.
